EXPLANATION

First, let's divide the polynomial f(x)=x4 by characteristic polynomial p(x)=x2+4x+3, using long division:

x2 − 4x + 13
x2+4x+3 x4|
x4 + 4x3 + 3x2
− 4x3 − 3x2
− 4x3 − 16x2 − 12x
13x2 + 12x
13x2 + 52x + 39
− 40x − 39

Therefore, we can write x4 as

x4=q(x)p(x)+(−40x−39), where q(x)=x2−4x+13. Replacing x with A, we have

A4=q(A)p(A)+(−40A−39I).

Now, according to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have p(A)=O. Therefore,

A4=q(A)p(A)+(−40A−39I)=q(A)⋅O+(−40A−39I)=−40A−39I.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Given that $\,A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value $p+q.$
after.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 3 \\ 3 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-8A+6I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-8A+6I) & =O \\ A-8I+6{A}^{-1} & =O \\ 6{A}^{-1} & =8I-A \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{4}{3}I-\frac{1}{6}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{4}{3},$ $q=-\frac{1}{6}$ and

$$
p+q=\frac{4}{3}+(-\frac{1}{6})=\frac{7}{6}.

content.knowledge_point: Expressing the Inverse of a Matrix as a Linear Combination of Its Powers
content.problem: Given that $\,A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value $p+q.$
content.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 3 \\ 3 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-8A+6I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-8A+6I) & =O \\ A-8I+6{A}^{-1} & =O \\ 6{A}^{-1} & =8I-A \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{4}{3}I-\frac{1}{6}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{4}{3},$ $q=-\frac{1}{6}$ and

$$
p+q=\frac{4}{3}+(-\frac{1}{6})=\frac{7}{6}.
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Given that $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -4 & 5\end{aligned}]$ and ${A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value of $p+q.$
after.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 3 \\ -4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(5-\lambda )+12 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +22 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-7A+22I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-7A+22I) & =O \\ A-7I+22{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{7}{22}I-\frac{1}{22}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{7}{22},$ $q=-\frac{1}{22},$ and 

$$
p+q=\frac{7}{22}+(-\frac{1}{22})=\frac{3}{11}.
$$

Given the matrix A=[42−6−4] and f(x)=x16−4x14+7x−3, find f(A).

b

decision.explanation: Direct multiplication gives A² = 4I. Therefore A¹⁶ − 4A¹⁴ = 4⁸I − 4·4⁷I = 0, so f(A) = 7A − 3I = [[25,14],[-42,-31]], matching option d.

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 2 \\ -6 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\  & =(4-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )+12 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:

|  | $\,\,{x}^{14}$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${x}^{2}-4\,$ | $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{16}\,-\,4{x}^{14}\,+\,7x\,-\,3}$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  | ${x}^{16}$ | $-$ | $4{x}^{14}$ |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  |  | $7x$ | $-$ | $3$ |

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\  & =q(x)p(x)+(7x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where $q(x)={x}^{14}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

$$
f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I).
$$

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I) \\  & =q(A)\cdot O+(7A-3I) \\  & =7A-3I \\  & =7[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}28 & 14 \\ -42 & -28\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 14 \\ -42 & -31\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
